# Prerequisites and conventions {#sec-conventions}

## Who these lectures are for

The reader is assumed to know calculus of one and several variables and linear algebra at the level of a first
university course, and to have met Newtonian mechanics. Nothing else is assumed: the foundations of mathematics
(Part I) develop set theory and topology, linear algebra, real and complex analysis, differential equations, Fourier
analysis, Hilbert spaces and operator theory, probability, differential geometry, Lie groups and their
representations, coset spaces and fibre bundles on explicit examples, and the foundations of physics (Part II)
develop, in this order, classical mechanics, classical electromagnetism, thermodynamics and statistical mechanics,
quantum mechanics, classical field theory, the Dirac equation, quantum field theory, gauge theories and symmetry
breaking, renormalisation, special and general relativity, supersymmetry and supergravity, each from its definitions. A reader who knows a chapter can skim its definitions and try its exercises.

## How the verification works

Every claim of the book, in a definition, a theorem, an example or the answer to an exercise, is a theorem of a Lean
library built on mathlib [@mathlib2020; @demoura2021]. The computational core of each proof is a Veriphy certificate
[@veriphy2026]: SageMath [@sagemath] finds the data of the certificate (coefficients, witnesses, closed forms,
eigenvectors), the Lean kernel checks the proof built from it, and only the Sage-free proof is committed, so the
library builds without Sage and contains no `sorry`. Physical laws are formalised as explicit mathematical models
(states and observables on Hilbert spaces, ensembles as probability measures, time-sliced path integrals, regularised
integrals and their flow equations) and the book's statements are theorems of those models.

The verification never interrupts the text. Below a block, a collapsed box labelled **Verification** opens like the
solution of an exercise. It always has the same shape: a **Veriphy** line names the recipe and the certificate, and the
certificate splits into its two halves, the **Lean** statement that the kernel checks and the **Sage** computation that
found the certificate's data. For the symmetry of the Christoffel symbols it reads:

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Recipe `calc_derivation`; certificate `christoffel_symm`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.christoffel_symm >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Lean part reproduces the docstring and the statement of the theorem, extracted from the Lean source when the book
is rendered. A part marked *Pending* belongs to a claim whose certificate is still being produced. @sec-registry-kaluza-klein-theories lists every claim with its Lean theorem and its recipe.

## Reading the blocks {#sec-conventions-blocks}

Every numbered block of the book is one of three kinds, told apart by the colour of its title. **Statements**, that
is, definitions, theorems, lemmas, propositions and corollaries, have a red title and stand in a light red box, which
also holds the statement's collapsed Verification box; each definition introduces exactly one notion. **Examples**
have a green title; every statement is followed by a run of them, of increasing complexity, which carry the figures
and their interactive versions. **Exercises** have a blue title; every statement is followed by a run of them, of
increasing difficulty, each with a folded solution, and every chapter ends with exercises that draw on all of its
sections. To keep the line of the argument visible, the examples of a statement are folded into one collapsed
**Examples** box placed right after it, and its exercises, with their solutions, into one collapsed **Exercises**
box; open them to work through the material. Solutions that use Sage show the committed script and its recorded
output.

## Coordinates, indices and signature {#sec-conventions-indices}

Spacetime is four-dimensional with coordinates $x^\mu$, $\mu = 0, 1, 2, 3$, and metric signature
$(+, -, -, -)$: $\eta_{\mu\nu} = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$, timelike vectors have $\eta(v, v) > 0$ and
spacelike ones $\eta(v, v) < 0$. Internal (compact) coordinates are $y^m$, and the full higher-dimensional
coordinates are $z^M = (x^\mu, y^m)$. Internal metrics are **negative definite**, so that the full metric
$\hat g_{MN}$ has signature $(+, -, \dots, -)$: the Kaluza-Klein ansatz reads $d\hat s^2 = g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu -
\phi^2(dy + A_\mu dx^\mu)^2$ on the circle and $g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - R^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$
on the sphere, and we write $h_{mn} = -\gamma_{mn}$ with $\gamma_{mn}$ the positive-definite round metric when the
internal geometry is discussed on its own (Part I treats Riemannian metrics, which are positive definite). Indices
are summed when repeated once up and once down.

The signature fixes the signs of the field-theory formulas: the Klein-Gordon equation is $(\Box + m^2)\phi = 0$
with $\Box = \eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu = \partial_t^2 - \nabla^2$, the scalar Lagrangian is
$\tfrac12\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\phi\,\partial_\nu\phi - V(\phi)$, the Maxwell and Yang-Mills Lagrangians are
$-\tfrac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ (unchanged by the signature, two indices being raised), the Dirac equation is
$(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - m)\psi = 0$ with $\{\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu\} = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}$, $(\gamma^0)^2 = 1$,
$(\gamma^i)^2 = -1$, and the Einstein-Hilbert Lagrangian is $-\tfrac{1}{16\pi G}\sqrt{-g}\,R$ with the curvature
conventions of @sec-conventions-curvature (the curvature scalar changes sign with the signature while the Riemann
and Ricci tensors do not). Under the ansatz above the circle reduction gives $\hat R = R + \tfrac14\phi^2
F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} - 2\phi^{-1}\Box\phi$ (Part III).

The Kaluza-Klein literature is split on the signature: @overduin1998 [Sec. 3], @tanii1998 and the CSDR reviews
[@manolakos2016, eq. 9; @manousselis2000] use $(+,-,-,-)$ as we do, while @duff1994 [p. 2], @duff2025 and
@martin1997 use $(-,+,+,+)$. Where we quote a formula from a source with the other signature, we say so and
convert: the rule is $g_{MN} \to -g_{MN}$, which leaves $\Gamma$, $R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}$, $R_{\mu\nu}$ and
$F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ unchanged and flips the signs of $R$, of $\Box$, of every $\eta^{\mu\nu}$ contraction with
an odd number of inverse metrics, and of the $\eta$ in the Clifford relation.

In the Lean library a chart is $\mathbb{R}^n$, written `Fin n → ℝ`, and a metric is the family of its components
$g_{ij}(x)$. The chart hypotheses (for instance $\sin\theta \neq 0$ on the sphere) exclude the points where the
coordinates degenerate; every statement holds on the chart domain.

## Connection and curvature {#sec-conventions-curvature}

The Levi-Civita connection has Christoffel symbols
$$
\Gamma^k_{ij} = \tfrac12 g^{kl} \left( \partial_i g_{lj} + \partial_j g_{li} - \partial_l g_{ij} \right),
$$ {#eq-christoffel-def}
the Riemann tensor is
$$
R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu \Gamma^\rho_{\nu\sigma} - \partial_\nu \Gamma^\rho_{\mu\sigma}
  + \Gamma^\rho_{\mu\lambda} \Gamma^\lambda_{\nu\sigma} - \Gamma^\rho_{\nu\lambda} \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\sigma},
$$ {#eq-riemann-def}
the Ricci tensor is $R_{\sigma\nu} = R^\rho{}_{\sigma\rho\nu}$ and the scalar curvature is
$R = g^{\sigma\nu} R_{\sigma\nu}$. With these signs the round unit sphere has $R = +2$ and the Einstein-Hilbert
action of general relativity is $S = \frac{1}{2\kappa^2} \int d^4x \sqrt{-g}\, R$ with $\kappa^2 = 8\pi G$. These
are the definitions coded in the Lean library (`CoordinateGeometry.christoffel`, `riemann`, `ricci`,
`scalarCurvature`), so every curvature statement is verified with exactly these signs.

## Lie algebras and gauge fields {#sec-conventions-lie}

Lie algebra generators are anti-Hermitian matrices $T_A$ with real structure constants,
$$
[T_A, T_B] = f_{AB}{}^C\, T_C .
$$ {#eq-structure-constants}
For $\mathfrak{so}(3) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2)$ the generators are the real matrices $(L_a)_{bc} = -\epsilon_{abc}$,
or equivalently $T_a = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ with the Pauli matrices, and $f_{ab}{}^c = \epsilon_{abc}$. This is
the convention of the CSDR literature [@kubyshin2003, Sec. 1; @chatzistavrakidis2007consistency, eq. 2.4], in which
the generators of a coset $S/R$ are split into $Q_i$ spanning $\mathfrak{r}$ and $Q_a$ spanning its complement.

A gauge field is a Lie-algebra-valued one-form $A = A_M\, dz^M$ with anti-Hermitian components, the covariant
derivative is $D_M = \partial_M + A_M$, and the field strength is
$$
F_{MN} = \partial_M A_N - \partial_N A_M + [A_M, A_N], \qquad F = dA + A \wedge A .
$$ {#eq-field-strength}
The Yang-Mills action is $S = \frac{1}{2 g^2} \int d^Dz \sqrt{|g|}\, \operatorname{Tr}(F_{MN} F^{MN})$ with the trace
in the fundamental representation and a positive coupling $g$. With $F_{MN} = F^a_{MN}T_a$ and
$\operatorname{Tr}(T_aT_b) = -\tfrac12\delta_{ab}$ this is $S = -\frac{1}{4g^2}\int d^Dz\sqrt{|g|}\,F^a_{MN}F^{a\,MN}$,
whose electric part $\tfrac{1}{2g^2}F^a_{0i}F^a_{0i}$ enters with the positive sign of a kinetic energy in the
signature $(+, -, \dots, -)$. @manolakos2016 and @manousselis2000 write $F_{MN} = \partial_M A_N - \partial_N A_M - [A_M, A_N]$ with
$D_M = \partial_M - A_M$, which is the same convention after $A \to -A$; @kubyshin2003 prints the commutator with a
minus sign in his eq. (9) but uses $F = dA + A\wedge A$ in his example (see the reading note). We never need a
gauge coupling inside the internal space, since CSDR fixes the internal components of $A$ in units of the coset
radius.

## Units

$\hbar = c = 1$. The five-dimensional gravitational coupling is $\hat\kappa^2 = 8\pi \hat G$; the circle has
circumference $2\pi R$. Lie algebra generators are normalised by $\operatorname{Tr}(T_a T_b) = -\tfrac12 \delta_{ab}$
in the fundamental representation of $SU(2)$ and $SU(3)$.
